The region set is constructed to separate two candidate explanations of transfer failure. Manavgat and Muğla are in the same country, in the same fire year, roughly 200 km apart, and share a baseline-year set; Bejís is in a different country, a different year, and about 2500 km away. If transferability were governed by geographic and climatic proximity, the Manavgat$\leftrightarrow$Muğla pair should transfer best. A \textbf{negative control} region (Kozan 2023, Türkiye), in which the burned area is dominated by agricultural stubble burning rather than wildfire, exists in the pipeline registry and is used only as a validity check on the admissibility gate described in Section~\ref{sec:3.3}; it is never used as a transfer partner. Its role is described in Section~\ref{sec:3.3} and its gate outcome is reported in Section~\ref{sec:4.1}.

\subsection{Burned-area label and the $\sim$500 m analysis grid}\label{sec:3.2}

The target variable is burned/unburned status derived from the MODIS MCD64A1 Collection 6 burned-area product, retrieved through Google Earth Engine. Active-fire detections (FIRMS) are never used as a target.

\textbf{Grid reconstruction.} MCD64A1 is a $\sim$500 m product on the MODIS sinusoidal grid, but it is exported from Earth Engine onto the 30 m EPSG:4326 reference grid used by the rest of the pipeline (\texttt{VALIDATION\_LABEL\_EXPORT\_SCALE = 30}, \texttt{core/config.py:262}), which duplicates each native $\sim$500 m observation across a block of 30 m pixels sharing its value. The analysis grid is therefore \emph{reconstructed} rather than native: the 30 m reference grid is partitioned into non-overlapping square blocks of \texttt{round(500 / 30) = 17 × 17} pixels (\texttt{step8a\_prepare\_500m\_modeling\_dataset.py:914 to 917}, using \texttt{STEP8A\_MCD64A1\_NATIVE\_CELL\_SIZE\_M = 500.0} and \texttt{STEP8A\_REFERENCE\_PIXEL\_SIZE\_M = 30.0}, \texttt{core/config.py:538 to 539}), giving a nominal cell edge of 510 m. This is an approximation of the true MODIS sinusoidal cell: it is anchored to the Landsat/EPSG:4326 reference grid rather than to the MODIS tile grid, and blocks at the AOI margin are truncated and therefore contain fewer than 289 constituent pixels. This is stated explicitly because it is a real, and reported, limitation of the label geometry rather than an incidental implementation detail. Each cell is identified by its integer block indices \texttt{row\_500m = row\_offset // 17}, \texttt{col\_500m = col\_offset // 17} (\texttt{step8a:920 to 936}); these indices are used to construct spatial cross-validation blocks and are never used as predictors.

The 30 m reference grid itself is the Landsat current-period median LST raster produced upstream, and every other continuous predictor is required to match it exactly in width, height, CRS and affine transform; a mismatch is a hard error and the pipeline never silently resamples (\texttt{step8a:613 to 643}). The two exceptions are documented and use nearest-neighbour resampling only, because both layers are categorical: land cover (\texttt{step8a:479 to 551}) and the MCD64A1 burn-date raster itself (\texttt{step8a:768 to 814}).

\textbf{Label assignment.} Within each 17$\times$17 block, only strictly positive burn-date day-of-year values are considered; zeros and no-data are ignored. A cell is unburned by default. If positive values exist, their modal day-of-year is taken as the cell's representative burn date, ties being broken in favour of the smaller value --- which, for the burned/unburned decision, means the conservative direction (\texttt{step8a:939 to 951}). The representative day-of-year is then converted to a calendar date and tested against the region's label window: if it falls inside the window the cell is labelled burned, otherwise the cell is retained as \textbf{unburned} and flagged \texttt{out\_of\_window\_burndate} (\texttt{step8a:1204 to 1248}). The fraction of positive sub-pixels agreeing with the modal date is recorded as a diagnostic (\texttt{burn\_date\_pixel\_agreement\_fraction}) but no agreement threshold is imposed; a single in-window positive sub-pixel is sufficient to label the cell burned.

The label never affects a cell's eligibility for modelling (Section~\ref{sec:3.5}). Unburned cells, all-no-data blocks and out-of-window cells all remain in the dataset as the negative class.

\textbf{Pre-label burn exclusion.} Optionally, cells that already show a burn detection in the interval between the start of the predictor window and the start of the label window are excluded from the analysis universe entirely, so that a predictor window cannot be contaminated by an earlier fire within the same season (\texttt{step8a:2592 to 2605}, using the exclusion manifest produced by the gate step). Excluded cells are marked \texttt{analysis\_eligible = False}; their raw labels are preserved for audit but they never enter modelling.

\subsection{Burned-landcover admissibility gate}\label{sec:3.3}

Before any predictor modelling, each region passes through a gate (\texttt{step6b\_burned\_landcover\_gate.py}) that answers one question: \textbf{of the cells labelled burned, what land cover dominates them?} The gate reads only the burn-date raster and the aligned land-cover raster, and reuses Step8A's block size, cell-identity function and land-cover class map verbatim, so its cells are identical to the modelling cells.

For each burned cell the modal ESA WorldCover class is taken. Regional fractions are then formed with the total burned-cell count as denominator: a natural-vegetation fraction (tree cover 10 + shrubland 20 + grassland 30) and a cropland fraction (class 40). The verdict rule is applied in order (\texttt{step6b:172 to 211}):

\begin{enumerate}
  \item fewer than \texttt{STEP6\_BURNED\_LANDCOVER\_GATE\_MIN\_POSITIVES = 30} burned cells $\rightarrow$ \emph{insufficient burned positives};
  \item natural-vegetation fraction $\ge$ 0.50 $\rightarrow$ \textbf{wildfire candidate --- pass};
  \item cropland fraction $\ge$ 0.50 $\rightarrow$ \emph{cropland-dominated control};
  \item otherwise $\rightarrow$ \emph{mixed or uncertain}.
\end{enumerate}

Thresholds are at \texttt{core/config.py:369 to 373}. The gate is diagnostic: a failing verdict does not halt the pipeline, and the gate output always carries \texttt{downstream\_authorized: False}, requiring explicit review. Its role in this study is to establish that the regions entering the transfer experiment are genuine forest-fire regions. Per-region verdicts and natural-vegetation fractions are read from each region's frozen \texttt{burned\_landcover\_gate.json} and reported in Section~\ref{sec:4.1}.

\textbf{Negative control.} A gate that every candidate region passes carries no information, so the threshold is calibrated against a region that should fail it. MCD64A1 does not distinguish the combustion of natural fuel from the deliberate burning of harvest residue: both are detected as burned area, and a model trained on the latter would be learning agricultural calendar rather than fire-relevant dryness. Kozan 2023 (Adana province, Türkiye) was therefore processed through the identical Step 1 to 6 pipeline as a negative control. It is not a wildfire region: its burned area lies in the Çukurova agricultural plain and is dominated by post-harvest stubble burning. The gate receives it blind --- it sees only the burn-date raster and the land-cover raster, with no regional label --- and the verdict follows from rule 3 above. The control is reported in Section~\ref{sec:4.1} and enters no modelling, transfer or diagnostic analysis; no Kozan number appears anywhere else in this paper.

\subsection{Predictor variables}\label{sec:3.4}

All dynamic predictors are composited over the region's predictor window; static predictors are time-invariant. Each is produced by a named upstream pipeline stage and delivered on the 30 m reference grid.

\textbf{Optical greenness (NDVI).} Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 surface reflectance, scaled by 0.0000275 with an offset of $-$0.2, is used to compute NDVI = (NIR $-$ Red)/(NIR + Red); pixels with a near-zero denominator or values outside [$-$1, 1] are masked (\texttt{core/config.py:89 to 103}). The predictor-window composite is a per-pixel \textbf{median}.

\textbf{Land surface temperature (Landsat).} The Landsat Level-2 surface temperature band is scaled by 0.00341802 with an offset of 149.0 K and converted to degrees Celsius. The predictor-window composite is again a per-pixel median (\texttt{current\_lst}, in \textdegree{}C); this raster also serves as the 30 m reference grid.

\textbf{LST anomaly.} A z-score of the current-window LST median against the baseline-years distribution for the same calendar window: \texttt{(current\_median − baseline\_mean) / baseline\_std} (\texttt{step5\_preprocess\_timeseries.py:837 to 847}). The anomaly is set to no-data where the baseline standard deviation is below \texttt{STEP5\_MIN\_BASELINE\_STD\_CELSIUS = 1.0} \textdegree{}C, where fewer than \texttt{STEP5\_MIN\_CURRENT\_VALID\_COUNT = 2} current observations exist, or where fewer than \texttt{STEP5\_MIN\_BASELINE\_VALID\_COUNT = 3} baseline observations exist. The result is dimensionless.

\textbf{TVDI and TVDI difference.} The Temperature-Vegetation Dryness Index is computed in the LST-NDVI feature space (\texttt{step5c\_tvdi.py}): the NDVI range [0, 1] is divided into \texttt{TVDI\_NDVI\_BIN\_COUNT = 20} bins; within each bin with at least \texttt{TVDI\_MIN\_PIXELS\_PER\_BIN = 30} valid pixels, the wet and dry edges are taken as the 2nd and 98th LST percentiles (\texttt{TVDI\_WET\_EDGE\_PERCENTILE = 2.0}, \texttt{TVDI\_DRY\_EDGE\_PERCENTILE = 98.0}); TVDI is then \texttt{(LST − wet\_edge) / (dry\_edge − wet\_edge)}, clamped to [0, 1], and set to no-data where the edge span is below \texttt{MIN\_TVDI\_EDGE\_SPAN\_C = 1.0} \textdegree{}C (\texttt{core/config.py:162 to 178}). \texttt{tvdi\_difference} is the current-window TVDI minus the baseline-years mean TVDI. A documented caveat applies to the latter: the baseline TVDI is formed from a single baseline LST mean raster combined with per-year NDVI, so its inter-annual variation derives from NDVI alone (\texttt{step5c\_tvdi.py:480 to 486}).

\textbf{Downscaled and fused LST.} To mitigate Landsat's sparse thermal revisit, a MODIS$\rightarrow$Landsat downscaling model is trained on the predictor window and applied to the full 30 m grid (\texttt{step7c}, \texttt{step7d}), yielding \texttt{downscaled\_lst} in \textdegree{}C, clipped to configured physical bounds. The downscaling stage is explicitly leakage-guarded: it never sees MCD64A1 or FIRMS labels, and is prevented from ingesting the anomaly, TVDI or TVDI-difference layers as inputs (\texttt{step7d\_predict\_downscaled\_lst.py:1 to 30}). A fused product (\texttt{fused\_lst}, \textdegree{}C) then combines observed Landsat LST with downscaled LST as \textbf{gap-fill only} --- valid observed pixels are never replaced or blended (\texttt{step7e\_fuse\_landsat\_downscaled\_lst.py:1 to 26}). A companion source mask records, per pixel, whether the fused value is observed, gap-filled or invalid; the corresponding per-cell fractions are retained as sensitivity diagnostics and are \textbf{never} used as predictors.

\textbf{Terrain.} Elevation (m a.s.l.) and slope (degrees, from \texttt{ee.Terrain.slope}) are derived from the Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (ESA, 30 m global digital surface model; \texttt{https://dataspace.copernicus.eu/explore-data/data-collections/copernicus-contributing-missions/collections-description/COP-DEM}, accessed 2026-08-08), accessed as the \texttt{COPERNICUS/DEM/GLO30} Earth Engine collection. USGS SRTMGL1 v003 is configured as a fallback should the preferred collection be unavailable (\texttt{core/config.py:61 to 80}); the frozen Step 2B metadata records \texttt{used\_fallback: false} for every region, so all reported elevation and slope values come from GLO-30 and the fallback was never exercised. Because GLO-30 is a mosaicked collection without a fixed projection, slope is computed on the DEM's native projection before reprojection, not after (\texttt{step2b\_dem.py:148 to 159}). Both bands are exported at 30 m.

\textbf{Land cover.} ESA WorldCover v200 (10 m native, 2021 epoch), nearest-neighbour aligned to the 30 m reference grid. Class codes: 10 tree cover, 20 shrubland, 30 grassland, 40 cropland, 50 built-up, 60 bare/sparse vegetation, 70 snow/ice, 80 permanent water, 90 herbaceous wetland, 95 mangroves, 100 moss/lichen.

\subsection{Cell-level aggregation, validity mask and analysis population}\label{sec:3.5}

\textbf{Aggregation.} For each continuous predictor and each 17$\times$17 block, the mean, median, standard deviation, valid-pixel count and valid-pixel fraction of the finite 30 m values are computed (\texttt{step8a:954 to 963}). Modelling uses the block \textbf{mean} of each predictor. For land cover, the modal class (\texttt{landcover\_dominant}) and per-class area fractions are computed over valid land-cover pixels within the block.

\textbf{Validity.} A cell is \texttt{valid\_for\_modeling} if and only if all of the following hold (\texttt{step8a:1399 to 1422}): it is analysis-eligible (not excluded as a pre-label burn); at least \texttt{STEP8A\_MIN\_30M\_VALID\_FRACTION = 0.3} of its 30 m pixels have simultaneously finite NDVI, elevation and slope; its aggregated NDVI, elevation and slope means are each finite; and it contains at least one valid land-cover pixel. Thermal predictors deliberately do \textbf{not} enter the validity test, so that thermal data availability cannot silently reshape the population differently for the two feature sets. The label likewise plays no part in the validity test --- a design point made explicit in the source, since requiring a valid burn date would collapse the dataset to burned-like cells.

\textbf{Analysis population.} The \textbf{primary} population is natural vegetation: cells that are \texttt{valid\_for\_modeling} and satisfy \texttt{burnable\_tree\_shrub\_grass}, defined as a combined tree + shrubland + grassland \textbf{area fraction $\ge$ \texttt{STEP8A\_BURNABLE\_FRACTION\_THRESHOLD} = 0.50} within the cell (\texttt{step8a:1326 to 1329}). Cropland is explicitly excluded from every burnable mask and only ever reported as its own fraction. Restricting to natural vegetation removes the confound in which agricultural stubble burning and bare-surface thermal contrast could be mistaken for wildfire skill; it is the scientifically defensible population for the transfer question, and --- as the analysis shows --- the choice materially changes the conclusion. The mixed population of all valid cells (\texttt{all\_valid}) is retained throughout as a \textbf{secondary sensitivity} analysis, and both populations are reported for every headline quantity.

Two definitional asymmetries are noted for transparency: the burnable mask is an \textbf{area-fraction} test, whereas the admissibility gate of Section~\ref{sec:3.3} uses the \textbf{modal} class; and the upstream within-region pipeline's own configured primary population is \texttt{all\_valid} (\texttt{STEP8B\_PRIMARY\_POPULATION}, \texttt{core/config.py:559}), whereas the transfer analysis reported here takes natural vegetation as primary. All comparisons in this paper --- within-region reference, naive transfer and adapted transfer alike --- are computed on the \emph{same} population and the \emph{same} classifier configuration, which is what makes the decomposition of Section~\ref{sec:3.12} valid.

\texttt{burnable\_tree\_shrub\_grass} is used exclusively as a population mask and is never a feature.

\subsection{Feature sets}\label{sec:3.6}

Two nested feature sets are compared (\texttt{step8b\_train\_baseline\_vs\_thermal\_model.py:121 to 135}):

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Baseline (4 predictors):} \texttt{ndvi\_mean}, \texttt{elevation\_mean}, \texttt{slope\_mean}, \texttt{landcover\_dominant}.
  \item \textbf{Thermal (10 predictors):} the baseline set plus \texttt{lst\_anomaly\_mean}, \texttt{current\_lst\_mean}, \texttt{current\_tvdi\_mean}, \texttt{tvdi\_difference\_mean}, \texttt{downscaled\_lst\_mean}, \texttt{fused\_lst\_mean}.
\end{itemize}

The thermal set is a strict superset of the baseline set, so the difference in performance between them is attributable to the six thermal channels alone. \texttt{landcover\_dominant} is the only categorical predictor.

\textbf{Table 2} (feature dictionary: variable, source product, producing pipeline stage, unit, temporal window, feature-set membership) is assembled from Section~\ref{sec:3.4}.

\subsection{Classifier and preprocessing}\label{sec:3.7}

All models are random forests with identical hyperparameters across the within-region, transfer and adaptation experiments (\texttt{step8b:420 to 429}):

\begin{verbatim}
RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_depth=None, min_samples_leaf=3,
                       class_weight="balanced", random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
\end{verbatim}

with scikit-learn defaults otherwise (\texttt{criterion="gini"}, \texttt{max\_features="sqrt"}, \texttt{min\_samples\_split=2}, bootstrap resampling of training rows). \texttt{class\_weight="balanced"} compensates for the strong class imbalance (burned prevalence of a few per cent). The configuration is chosen once and never tuned against any evaluation the paper reports; a second, unweighted profile with \texttt{min\_samples\_leaf=2} is retained solely as a sensitivity check.

Preprocessing is a scikit-learn \texttt{Pipeline} fitted \textbf{inside} each training fold (or, for transfer, on the source region only), so that no imputation or encoding statistic is derived from evaluation data (\texttt{step8b:449 to 467}): numeric predictors are median-imputed; \texttt{landcover\_dominant} is mode-imputed and one-hot encoded with \texttt{handle\_unknown="ignore"}, so that a land-cover class present in the evaluation set but absent from the training set produces an all-zero indicator row rather than an error. This is what makes the one-hot column space consistent between regions in the transfer experiments: it is fixed by the source region. No feature scaling is applied in the within-region models, as the classifier is scale-invariant.

\subsection{Spatial-block cross-validation and block-size robustness}\label{sec:3.8}

Within-region evaluation uses \textbf{spatially blocked} cross-validation. Contiguous square blocks of \texttt{B × B} analysis cells are formed at a fixed origin from the grid indices, \texttt{block\_row = row\_500m // B}, \texttt{block\_col = col\_500m // B} (\texttt{step8b:277 to 306}), and the resulting block identifier is used as the grouping variable in \texttt{StratifiedGroupKFold} with \texttt{n\_splits = 5}, \texttt{shuffle=True} and \texttt{random\_state = 42} (\texttt{step8b:309 to 414}; \texttt{core/config.py:554 to 556}). Blocks are therefore never split between training and test folds, and class stratification is preserved across folds. Fold construction is guarded: at least two test folds must contain a positive, and the pipeline is explicitly forbidden from ever falling back to a random row-wise split.

Both feature sets are fitted on the \textbf{same folds}, so the baseline-versus-thermal comparison is paired by construction. Out-of-fold predicted probabilities are assembled into a single vector per feature set, covering every cell exactly once, and metrics are computed once on the concatenated out-of-fold vector rather than averaged over folds (\texttt{step8b:519 to 690}).

\textbf{Block size and robustness.} The pipeline's default block size is \texttt{STEP8B\_SPATIAL\_BLOCK\_SIZE\_CELLS = 2}, i.e. 2 $\times$ 2 cells $\approx$ 1 km. Because the appropriate blocking scale is not knowable a priori and short-range spatial autocorrelation can survive fine blocking, the whole within-region analysis is repeated at \textbf{B = 2, 10 and 20 cells ($\approx$ 1, 5 and 10 km)}, on both populations. A thermal increment that persists as blocks coarsen is evidence of genuine spatial generalisation rather than of neighbour leakage; the trade-off is that coarser blocking also reduces the number of independent groups available for cross-validation and for bootstrap resampling, which widens the intervals.

\textbf{Metrics.} Threshold-free discrimination is reported as ROC-AUC and PR-AUC (average precision); the Brier score is computed as a calibration diagnostic. Threshold-dependent quantities (balanced accuracy, precision, recall, F1) are recorded at a fixed 0.5 cut-off within regions but are not used for the paper's claims (\texttt{step8b:480 to 503}). The primary quantity of interest is the paired difference $\Delta$AUC = AUC(thermal) $-$ AUC(baseline) on the same out-of-fold predictions.

\subsection{Spatial-block bootstrap uncertainty}\label{sec:3.9}

Uncertainty is quantified by a \textbf{spatial-block bootstrap} operating on stored predictions, with no refitting (\texttt{step8c\_spatial\_block\_bootstrap\_uncertainty.py}). The resampling unit is the spatial block, not the cell: in each replicate, \texttt{n\_blocks} blocks are drawn with replacement from the \texttt{n\_blocks} unique blocks, and a block drawn \emph{k} times contributes all of its cells \emph{k} times (\texttt{step8c:278 to 351}). Resampling cells individually would treat spatially autocorrelated neighbours as independent and produce intervals that are far too narrow --- an error we made and corrected during this study (Section~\ref{sec:3.12}).

The number of replicates is 1000 and the seed is 42 (\texttt{core/config.py:574 to 575}). Intervals are \textbf{equal-tailed percentile} intervals at the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles; no bias correction or acceleration (BCa) is applied. Replicates in which a resample contains only one class are recorded and excluded from the percentiles rather than silently redrawn; a warning is raised if more than 10\% of replicates are invalid.

The bootstrap is \textbf{paired}: within each replicate, both the baseline and thermal probability vectors are evaluated on the identical resampled index and the difference is formed inside the replicate, so the interval is on the distribution of the paired $\Delta$AUC. The same paired construction is used in the transfer experiments, where a single set of resampled target blocks per replicate is shared by all probability series (within-region reference, raw transfer, z-scored transfer, CORAL transfer) so that they remain directly comparable.

Following the pipeline's own reporting policy, no classical p-values or significance tests are reported. A result is described as having \textbf{positive bootstrap support} when the 95\% percentile interval for $\Delta$AUC excludes zero, and as \textbf{uncertain} otherwise; this is a statement about an interval, not a hypothesis test.

Block sizes used for the bootstrap match the analysis they accompany: B = 2 for the transfer scores, B matched to the cross-validation blocking (2, 10, 20) for the within-region robustness analysis, and B = 10 ($\approx$ 5 km) for the univariate concept-shift diagnostic of Section~\ref{sec:3.12}.

\subsection{Cross-region transfer protocol}\label{sec:3.10}

For each ordered pair of regions (source $\rightarrow$ target), a model is fitted on the \textbf{entire} source region --- all cells in the analysis population, no held-out fold --- and applied to the entire target region. All ordered pairs among the completed regions are evaluated in both directions.

Every fitted component is derived from the source region only: the numeric imputation medians, the categorical mode, the one-hot category vocabulary, and the random forest itself. The target region enters the computation exactly once, at \texttt{predict\_proba}. There is no pooled fitting, no target-derived imputation, no target fine-tuning, no calibration on the target, and no coordinate or region-identity feature (\texttt{step9b\_run\_cross\_region\_transfer.py:230 to 236, 370 to 381}). The classifier, hyperparameters, seed and feature contract are imported from the within-region stage rather than redefined, so the transfer model is the same model.

Feature harmonisation across regions requires no separate alignment step: the shared feature list is frozen and validated by an audit stage that fails on any schema mismatch, and the source-fitted one-hot encoder with \texttt{handle\_unknown="ignore"} guarantees identical column ordering and dimension at target-prediction time. Land-cover classes present in the target but not the source encode to zero.

Both source and target must contain at least 30 positive and 30 negative cells in the population being evaluated, otherwise the pair is skipped.

\textbf{Target metrics} are threshold-free: ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, with spatial-block bootstrap intervals as in Section~\ref{sec:3.9}, computed on the target region's blocks. A ROC-AUC below 0.5 is reported as such and is interpreted as an anti-predictive transfer --- the source-learned ordering is systematically inverted in the target --- rather than being folded to \texttt{max(AUC, 1 − AUC)}. Both the baseline and the thermal feature set are fitted and evaluated under this protocol for every ordered direction, so the per-direction paired baseline-versus-thermal transfer contrast reported in the Results is a read-only extraction from these frozen outputs --- point estimates from the transfer stage's \texttt{baseline\_metrics}/\texttt{thermal\_metrics}, and paired $\Delta$AUC intervals from the transfer bootstrap's \texttt{delta\_roc\_auc} field, which evaluates both probability series on identical resampled target blocks as in Section~\ref{sec:3.9} (extraction script \texttt{paper/baseline\_vs\_thermal.mjs}; no new models fitted).

\subsection{Label-blind domain adaptation}\label{sec:3.11}

Three transfer variants are compared. All are strictly \textbf{label-blind}: the target frame is structurally stripped of the response before adaptation, and an assertion fails the run if a label column is present (\texttt{step10b\_label\_blind\_adaptation.py:71 to 79}; \texttt{core/step10\_shared.py:243 to 250}). No adaptation function accepts labels as an argument.

\textbf{(a) Raw.} The source-fitted model applied directly to untransformed target features (Section~\ref{sec:3.10}).

\textbf{(b) Region-wise z-score.} Each region's numeric features are standardised using \textbf{its own} statistics: \texttt{z = (x − μ\_region) / σ\_region}, with the mean and standard deviation computed over non-missing values only and \texttt{ddof = 0} (\texttt{step10\_shared.py:145 to 173}). A near-constant feature (σ < 10$^{-12}$) has its divisor set to 1 and the substitution is recorded. Missing values are filled with the region's own mean, hence map to exactly zero after transformation. The categorical land-cover predictor is left untouched. Source statistics come from source data and target statistics from target data; the two regions are never pooled. The classifier is then refitted on the z-scored source and applied to the z-scored target. This variant removes first- and second-order marginal offsets between regions --- the simplest possible self-calibration.

\textbf{(c) CORAL after region-wise z-score.} Starting from the z-scored features of (b), the source covariance is aligned to the target covariance by the standard CORAL whitening-recolouring map (\texttt{step10\_shared.py:186 to 220}):

\begin{verbatim}
C_s = cov(X_s^z) + λI ,   C_t = cov(X_t^z) + λI
A   = C_s^(−1/2) · C_t^(1/2)
X_s* = X_s^z · A
\end{verbatim}

with covariances computed at \texttt{ddof = 0} and matrix powers obtained by symmetric eigendecomposition with eigenvalues floored at 10$^{-12}$. The regularisation is \texttt{STEP10\_CORAL\_LAMBDA = 1e-5} (\texttt{core/config.py:697}). Critically, \textbf{the transform is applied to the source only}; the target remains exactly as in (b). The classifier is refitted on the aligned source and applied to the unchanged z-scored target.

\textbf{On the choice of $\lambda$.} The canonical CORAL formulation adds the identity ($\lambda$ = 1) to each covariance, but it is defined for unstandardised features. Here CORAL is applied \emph{after} region-wise standardisation, so each feature already has unit variance and adding the full identity doubles the diagonal, imposing shrinkage strong enough to erase the covariance structure the alignment is meant to exploit. With only nine numeric features and thousands of cells per region, the covariances are well estimated and minimal regularisation is appropriate. Because this is a defensible but not inevitable choice, $\lambda$ sensitivity is assessed on the four Bejís$\leftrightarrow$Muğla and Manavgat$\leftrightarrow$Muğla directions over a nine-value grid from 0 to 10$^{-1}$ (0, 10$^{-8}$ \ldots{} 10$^{-1}$); the resulting spread in transfer AUC is at most 0.008 within any direction (Section~\ref{sec:4.7}d). The sweep does not extend to $\lambda$ = 1 or to the Montiferru and Evia directions, so conclusions for those directions rest on the default $\lambda$ = 10$^{-5}$ alone.

The order of operations for variant (c) is thus: region-wise z-score of both regions $\rightarrow$ CORAL alignment of the source numerics only $\rightarrow$ the standard median-imputation + one-hot pipeline $\rightarrow$ random-forest fit on source $\rightarrow$ prediction on target.

\subsection{Transfer-gap decomposition and concept-shift diagnostic}\label{sec:3.12}

\textbf{Decomposition.} For each ordered pair, the transfer deficit is decomposed against the target region's own within-region performance:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \texttt{total\_gap      = AUC\_within(target) − AUC\_raw(source→target)}
  \item \texttt{recovered      = AUC\_adapted(source→target) − AUC\_raw(source→target)}
  \item \texttt{concept\_remaining = AUC\_within(target) − AUC\_adapted(source→target)}
\end{itemize}

where \texttt{AUC\_within} is the target region's own spatially blocked out-of-fold thermal ROC-AUC. All three terms are computed on the \textbf{same population, same feature set, same classifier configuration and same block size}, which is what makes them commensurable; a decomposition assembled from components with differing populations or classifier settings would not be interpretable.

The \texttt{recovered} term is defined using the \textbf{best-performing label-blind method} among (b) and (c), because the question it answers is "how much of the gap \emph{can} label-free alignment close?", whose answer is bounded by the best available label-free method. The weaker method's decomposition is reported as a secondary row rather than discarded, since choosing the weaker method as the numerator would understate the recoverable fraction and overstate concept shift.

\textbf{Concept-shift diagnostic.} To identify the mechanism behind the residual, a \textbf{signed} univariate ROC-AUC is computed for every numeric feature against the burned label, independently in each region's analysis population. The AUC is deliberately \emph{not} folded to \texttt{max(AUC, 1 − AUC)}, so that the direction of association is preserved: a value above 0.5 means higher feature values are associated with burning, below 0.5 means the opposite. A feature is said to show a \textbf{point reversal} when its univariate AUC falls on opposite sides of 0.5 in the two regions, and a \textbf{bootstrap-supported reversal} only when the two regions' spatial-block bootstrap intervals are additionally \textbf{disjoint}.

The block size for this diagnostic is B = 10 cells ($\approx$ 5 km). An earlier version of the analysis used B = 2 ($\approx$ 1 km) and, by ignoring short-range spatial autocorrelation, produced intervals roughly four times too narrow, which wrongly promoted several point reversals to bootstrap-supported. The correction is reported here because it materially weakened one of the study's own claims: at the appropriate blocking scale, far fewer reversals survive as statistically supported, and the manuscript reports the conservative result.

The logical role of this diagnostic is specific. Region-wise standardisation and covariance alignment can only translate, scale and rotate the feature distribution; neither can invert the sign of a feature's association with the response. A bootstrap-supported reversal is therefore direct evidence for a shift component that no label-free alignment can repair, and connects the empirical decomposition to a mechanism.

\subsection{Leakage control, sensitivity analyses and reproducibility}\label{sec:3.13}

\textbf{Leakage control.} An explicit forbidden-column set is enforced at every model fit, and its violation raises rather than warns (\texttt{step8b:140 to 159, 265 to 271, 450}). It contains the response itself and every column carrying label information --- \texttt{burn\_date}, \texttt{burn\_month}, \texttt{burn\_day\_of\_year}, \texttt{label\_source}, \texttt{burn\_date\_pixel\_agreement\_fraction}, \texttt{out\_of\_window\_burndate} --- together with \texttt{lon}, \texttt{lat}, \texttt{cell\_id}, \texttt{row\_500m}, \texttt{col\_500m}, the validity columns, and the fused-LST provenance columns (\texttt{source\_mask\_majority}, \texttt{observed\_fraction}, \texttt{gapfilled\_fraction}, \texttt{invalid\_source\_fraction}). The transfer stage additionally forbids \texttt{experiment\_id}, \texttt{region\_key}, \texttt{spatial\_block\_id} and \texttt{fold\_id}.

Coordinates are excluded because a fire scar is a spatially compact object: with longitude and latitude available, a sufficiently flexible model can memorise the scar's location instead of learning any relationship with the surface state. Grid indices are used only to construct cross-validation blocks and bootstrap groups. The natural-vegetation mask is used only to define the population. The fused-LST provenance fractions are retained for a sensitivity analysis --- performance restricted to cells with a low gap-filled fraction --- but never as predictors.

\textbf{Sensitivity analyses.} Every headline result is repeated across: two analysis populations (natural vegetation, primary; all valid cells, secondary); two random-forest profiles (the primary weighted \texttt{min\_samples\_leaf = 3} configuration and an unweighted \texttt{min\_samples\_leaf = 2} profile); three spatial-block sizes for the within-region analysis ($\approx$ 1, 5, 10 km); four CORAL regularisation values; and both feature sets. Where a conclusion depends on one of these choices, the dependence is reported rather than resolved by selecting the favourable setting.

\textbf{Reproducibility.} All randomness uses seed 42 --- model \texttt{random\_state}, cross-validation shuffling and bootstrap generators alike --- and the bootstrap uses 1000 replicates throughout. The transfer and adaptation analysis is executed in a dedicated Python environment separate from the upstream pipeline environment; because random-forest fits are not bit-identical across scikit-learn versions, the analysis includes an explicit reproduction check in which the within-region models are refitted in the new environment and compared against the frozen upstream outputs, and the independently implemented adaptation is compared against the pipeline's own implementation. All numbers reported in this paper were produced under, or verified against, scikit-learn 1.9.0: two frozen transfer probes reproduce to four decimal places under 1.9.0 but move by +0.021 and +0.026 AUC under 1.7.2 with byte-identical data, pipeline and seed, so cross-region point estimates carry an implementation tolerance of roughly $\pm$0.02 to 0.03 unless the exact library version is fixed --- within-region AUCs reproduce to $\sim$4 decimals across versions (\texttt{paper/sklearn\_version\_sensitivity.md}; probe script \texttt{paper/pairwise\_check.py}).

The reproduction check was executed on the final five-region set by the pipeline author, and its record is archived with this manuscript (\texttt{paper/reproduction\_check/reproduction\_check\_5region.json}, SHA-256 \texttt{7f7e41f5…09c8be}; commit \texttt{48b56e7}, Python 3.12.3, scikit-learn 1.9.0, pandas 3.0.2, NumPy 2.4.4, primary population \texttt{burnable\_tree\_shrub\_grass}). Two families of comparison were re-executed against the frozen outputs. The within-region arm refitted \texttt{step8b}'s baseline and thermal models on the frozen Step 8A parquet of each of the five experiments and compared ROC-AUC and PR-AUC --- twenty comparisons, all twenty produced, \textbf{maximum absolute difference exactly 0}. The transfer arm regenerated the label-blind CORAL predictions and re-evaluated them for all twenty directed region pairs, again in both model families and both metrics --- eighty comparisons over twenty directions, none missing, \textbf{maximum absolute ROC-AUC difference 1.6$\times$10$^{-7}$} (largest case Montiferru$\rightarrow$Manavgat, thermal: 0.6060780 against 0.6060778); sixty-nine of the eighty comparisons were bit-identical and the remaining eleven differed by 1.6$\times$10$^{-7}$ or less.

The tolerance against which these differences are judged is not a criterion chosen for this report. It is the repository's own pre-existing Step 10C fail-fast reproduction criterion --- absolute difference $\le$ 1$\times$10$^{-6}$, defined in \texttt{src/step10c\_paired\_evaluation\_bootstrap.py} --- applied unchanged, and the check record states this explicitly. Both arms fall inside it, the within-region arm by exact equality. The reported \texttt{PASS} is a technical-completion status covering cohort resolution, comparison coverage and input-hash agreement; the achieved numerical differences are reported separately, as above, rather than folded into that status.

What this check does and does not establish should be stated plainly. Because it re-executes the pipeline in the same library environment that produced the frozen outputs, the exact-zero within-region agreement demonstrates determinism and the absence of undeclared state --- that the recorded numbers are regenerable from the recorded inputs, hashes included --- rather than robustness to a change of environment. The residual 10$^{-7}$-scale differences in the transfer arm arise from re-derived rather than re-read intermediate quantities, not from a different library stack. Cross-version behaviour is established separately and is far coarser: the $\pm$0.02 to 0.03 implementation tolerance quoted above, from the 1.9.0-against-1.7.2 probes. The two statements are complementary and neither substitutes for the other.

Two further properties of the record are stated for completeness. First, the five-region cohort was resolved by three independent routes --- the experiment registry restricted to canonical records (those carrying no \texttt{superseded\_by} key, which drops the legacy Evia AOI of Section~\ref{sec:3.16.1} and the superseded Muğla calendar-shift record) and with non-cohort roles removed, the ERA5-Land diagnostic's \texttt{DEFAULT\_EXPERIMENTS} constant, and the frozen multi-AOI synthesis manifest --- and all three return the same ordered set (\texttt{routes\_agree: true}); the two deliberate exclusions by role are Kozan 2023 as \texttt{negative\_control} and the second Muğla event as \texttt{temporal\_transfer\_wildfire} (Sections~\ref{sec:3.1}, \ref{sec:3.3}, \ref{sec:3.16.4}). The roles and the supersession links are as recorded in \texttt{core/regions.py}. Second, two unordered region pairs carry duplicate Step 10 namespaces on disk under reversed directory orderings with distinct analysis identifiers (Bejís-Muğla and Manavgat-Muğla); the reference artefact was selected by the frozen synthesis manifest rather than by directory listing, and the check record names both the paths present and the one used for each pair. No file belonging to the upstream pipeline or to previously frozen outputs was modified by this analysis.

\textbf{Data and code availability.} The satellite inputs are all public and are obtained through Google Earth Engine: MODIS MCD64A1 Collection 6 burned area, MODIS land surface temperature, Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 surface reflectance and surface temperature, Copernicus DEM GLO-30, and ESA WorldCover v200. No data were collected by the authors and no restricted or licensed data were used; the region definitions, date windows and thresholds given in this section are sufficient to regenerate every input from these sources.

The full processing pipeline (Steps 1 to 10), its configuration constants, and the frozen numeric outputs on which every reported number rests are publicly available at \texttt{https://github.com/emrehann17/satellite-thermal-digital-twin}. The repository is the authoritative source for the file and line references cited throughout this section. Analysis code is released under the repository's stated licence (MIT); no digital object identifier is minted for this release, and readers should cite the repository URL together with the commit identifier corresponding to the version of record.

\subsection{Transferability diagnostics versus transfer}\label{sec:3.14}

To test whether any pre-transfer measure of region similarity predicts transfer outcome, twenty candidate diagnostics from four families --- marginal predictor-distribution measures P(x), burned-niche overlap P(x|y=1), fire-regime spatial structure P(y), and conditional feature-response direction P(y|x) --- are each evaluated against the same target quantity under one common correlation framework.

\subsubsection{Rank-correlation framework}\label{sec:3.14.1}

The target quantity is the raw thermal transfer ROC-AUC of Section~\ref{sec:3.10} on the natural-vegetation population, over the 20 ordered directions (12 for measures available only on the four-region subset excluding Montiferru). For each diagnostic, Spearman's $\rho$ and Kendall's τ-b (tie-corrected) are computed against the transfer AUCs. Uncertainty uses a \textbf{pair-based bootstrap}: the unordered region pairs (10, or 6 for the subset) are resampled with replacement, and every sampled pair contributes \textbf{both} of its ordered directions, so the two directions of a pair --- which share geography and data --- are never treated as independent draws. 2,000 replicates are used with equal-tailed percentile 95\% intervals; replicates yielding degenerate (undefined) rank correlations are excluded and counted. All resampling is seeded from 42 with fixed per-measure offsets and implemented with the mulberry32 PRNG in Node.js --- fully deterministic, though not bit-identical to NumPy's generator (\texttt{paper/regime\_correlation.mjs}, \texttt{paper/niche\_corr.mjs}, \texttt{paper/conditional\_similarity.mjs}). Because the effective sample is 10 (or 6) unordered pairs that share member regions, power is low; a null result is reported as "not shown to order transfer", never as "shown not to".

\subsubsection{Marginal measures and the domain classifier}\label{sec:3.14.2}

Six marginal diagnostics are consumed unchanged from the upstream marginal/area-of-applicability audit (12 directed pairs, four-region subset; \texttt{drive\_new/diagnostics/marginal\_aoa\_completion/4b2a1c86…/comparison/marginal\_diagnostics\_with\_transfer.csv}): target mean and 95th-percentile predictor-space dissimilarity, fraction of target cells inside the weighted area of applicability, and fraction inside the unweighted support (all directed), plus climatic distance and geographic centroid geodesic distance (symmetric). Marginal separability is additionally measured for all ten pairs by a \textbf{domain classifier} trained to distinguish source from target cells: the same 10-predictor feature contract (\texttt{step9\_shared\_baseline\_thermal\_v1}), the step8b preprocessing pipeline reused unmodified, and the random-forest configuration of Section~\ref{sec:3.7}, evaluated as spatially blocked out-of-fold ROC-AUC using \texttt{StratifiedGroupKFold} over deterministic 10-cell ($\approx$5 km) blocks namespaced per region (5 splits, seed 42, strict zero-overlap folds), with a paired two-domain spatial-block bootstrap (1,000 replicates, seed 42, blocks resampled with replacement independently within each domain). Burned labels are never used. Design read from \texttt{drive\_new/diagnostics/domain\_classifier\_audit/comparison/manifest.json} and the per-pair manifests.

\subsubsection{Burned-niche overlap}\label{sec:3.14.3}

Niche overlap compares the two regions' burned-cell feature distributions, P(x|y=1), using burned cells of the primary population only (\texttt{valid\_for\_modeling} ∧ \texttt{burnable\_tree\_shrub\_grass} ∧ \texttt{burned = 1}; no unburned variant by design). Schoener's D = 1 $-$ ½Σ|p $-$ q| and Warren's I = 1 $-$ ½Σ(√p $-$ √q)$^{2}$ are computed (a) per numeric feature on 1-D histograms with 50 shared bins spanning the \textbf{global} range of all five regions' burned cells, averaged over the nine features, and (b) on a 20 $\times$ 20 histogram over the first two components of a global PCA fitted to the pooled, globally standardised (ddof = 0) burned cells of all five regions, with missing values imputed by the pooled median. The Mahalanobis distance between standardised burned centroids uses the pooled covariance ((n\_a $-$ 1)S\_a + (n\_b $-$ 1)S\_b)/(n\_a + n\_b $-$ 2) over the nine features. All measures are symmetric per unordered pair (\texttt{paper/niche\_overlap.py}; correlation with transfer via \texttt{paper/niche\_corr.mjs}).

\subsubsection{Conditional sign-agreement index}\label{sec:3.14.4}

For each region a nine-dimensional vector of \textbf{signed} univariate AUCs (Section~\ref{sec:3.12}: the probability that a burned cell carries the higher feature value; never folded about 0.5) is taken, with its $\approx$5 km-block bootstrap intervals, from the upstream five-region feature-stability table (\texttt{drive\_new/diagnostics/multi\_aoi\_transfer\_synthesis/<five-region set>/multi\_aoi\_feature\_stability.csv}, step9g family). Pair-level measures: sign-agreement count and fraction (features whose AUC $-$ 0.5 signs match), the Spearman correlation between the two vectors, and the cosine similarity of the (AUC $-$ 0.5) vectors; each is also computed restricted to \textbf{supported} features --- those whose bootstrap interval excludes 0.5 in \emph{both} regions. Consistency is enforced: per-region vectors must be identical across every pair row, and the supported-reversal set must reproduce the upstream \texttt{reversal\_status} flags exactly (\texttt{paper/conditional\_similarity.mjs}). Unlike every marginal, niche and regime measure, this index requires burned labels (or a labelled probe) in \textbf{both} regions: it diagnoses concept alignment and is not a label-free deployment screen.

\subsubsection{Fire-regime structure}\label{sec:3.14.5}

Burned-area spatial structure, P(y), is summarised by connected components of burned natural-vegetation cells, computed with 8-connectivity on the integer grid indices \texttt{row\_500m}/\texttt{col\_500m}. Per region: component count, largest-component share, and the effective component count --- the inverse Simpson index of component size shares, 1/Σ s\_k$^{2}$. The pair-level regime distance is |$\Delta$ log(effective count)| (primary) and |$\Delta$ largest share| (secondary), both symmetric. The implementation was verified to reproduce the upstream burned-pattern audit ("Rejim" table) exactly in all five regions --- component counts and largest/second component sizes identically, shares and effective counts to 1 $\times$ 10$^{-4}$ (\texttt{paper/burned\_components.mjs}).

\subsection{Interventions}\label{sec:3.15}

\subsubsection{Pooled multi-region training (leave-one-region-out)}\label{sec:3.15.1}

For each held-out target region, the other four regions' primary (natural-vegetation) populations are pooled and a single model is trained on the pool and evaluated on the untouched target, for both feature sets. The classifier is exactly that of Section~\ref{sec:3.7}, and preprocessing mirrors the transfer stage: numeric medians fitted on the pooled training set, mode-filled land cover expanded to indicator columns from the training vocabulary so that unseen target classes encode to zero. Two variants are run: raw features, and region-wise z-score in which every region --- the target included --- is standardised with its own mean and σ (ddof = 0, numeric features only), i.e. the label-free definition of Section~\ref{sec:3.11}(b). Target metrics are ROC-AUC, PR-AUC (reported against its no-skill base, the prevalence) and Brier, with a $\approx$5 km spatial-block bootstrap on the target (blocks \texttt{row\_500m//10} $\times$ \texttt{col\_500m//10}, 1,000 replicates, NumPy \texttt{default\_rng(42)}, single-class replicates excluded) (\texttt{paper/loro\_pooled.py}). The analysis was run under scikit-learn 1.9.0 only after two frozen pairwise transfers were reproduced to four decimal places in the same environment (\texttt{paper/pairwise\_check.py}; Section~\ref{sec:3.13}).

\subsubsection{Removal of direction-reversing features}\label{sec:3.15.2}

Four thermal-model configurations are compared: full (all 10 predictors, order preserved from the shared feature contract), minus \texttt{elevation\_mean}, minus \texttt{lst\_anomaly\_mean}, and minus both --- the two features being exactly the bootstrap-supported reversal set under the supported-reversal criterion of Section~\ref{sec:3.14.4}. The pipeline replicates step8b/step9b verbatim (same imputers, one-hot encoding, classifier and seed), and \textbf{hard parity assertions} abort the run on any deviation of the full configuration from the frozen outputs --- tolerance 5 $\times$ 10$^{-4}$ against the 20 step9b transfer AUCs and 1 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ against the step8c within-region out-of-fold AUCs; the observed deviations were 0.0000 everywhere. Within-region evaluation reuses the spatially blocked out-of-fold protocol of Section~\ref{sec:3.8} (2-cell blocks, \texttt{StratifiedGroupKFold}, seed 42). All deltas (configuration minus full) are formed inside each replicate of a paired $\approx$5 km-block bootstrap (10-cell blocks, 1,000 replicates, \texttt{default\_rng(42)}), so every interval is on the paired difference (\texttt{paper/feature\_drop.py}; report \texttt{paper/feature\_drop\_transfer.md}).

\subsection{Additional sensitivity designs}\label{sec:3.16}

\subsubsection{Evia AOI (legacy versus extended)}\label{sec:3.16.1}

North Evia exists in two AOI definitions with identical predictor and label windows: the legacy 0.40\textdegree{} $\times$ 0.40\textdegree{} box and the canonical extended 0.80\textdegree{} $\times$ 0.60\textdegree{} box (Table~\ref{tab:1}), whose $\approx$3$\times$ larger area leaves the burned scar essentially unchanged while reducing prevalence substantially (Section~\ref{sec:4.1}). Both AOIs were processed through the full pipeline, and both transfer arms (baseline and thermal, Section~\ref{sec:3.10}) were run for every Evia-involved direction under each AOI (\texttt{drive\_new/cross\_region/<pair>/step9b/cross\_region\_transfer\_metrics.json} for the legacy and extended pair folders). The extended AOI is canonical everywhere in this paper; the legacy AOI is retained \textbf{only} to test whether AOI extent and the induced prevalence change alter any transfer conclusion.

\subsubsection{Montiferru tree+shrub population}\label{sec:3.16.2}

Montiferru is the weakest admissibility-gate pass (burned cropland fraction 0.274), so a stricter population variant excluding grassland is examined: \texttt{burnable\_tree\_shrub}, present alongside \texttt{burnable\_tree\_shrub\_grass} in the frozen within-region bootstrap populations (\texttt{drive\_new/experiments/montiferru\_2021/step8c/step8c\_bootstrap\_metrics.json}, \texttt{bootstrap\_ci\_by\_population}) and in the transfer bootstrap groups of every Montiferru pair (\texttt{drive\_new/cross\_region/montiferru\_2021\_\_*/step9c/cross\_region\_bootstrap\_metrics.json}). The within-region thermal $\Delta$AUC and the eight Montiferru-involved cross-region thermal-versus-baseline deltas are compared between the two populations, reading the frozen outputs only; no new models are fitted for this check.

\subsubsection{Predictor-window closure}\label{sec:3.16.3}

A predictor-timing sensitivity, described here as documented in each region's frozen comparison report (\texttt{drive\_new/diagnostics/window\_closure\_region/<region>/<hash>/\_production/<region>/compare/report/window\_closure\_comparison.md} for Bejís, Muğla, Evia-extended and Montiferru; \texttt{drive\_new/diagnostics/window\_closure\_sensitivity/manavgat\_2021/compare/report/window\_closure\_comparison.md} for Manavgat). Three variants --- canonical, closure 7 days earlier, closure 14 days earlier --- move \textbf{both} ends of the predictor window together so the window length is preserved; the label window is frozen and identical in every variant. One exact common cohort (the intersection of analysis-eligible, primary-population, valid rows of every variant, after removing shared pre-label-censored cells) and one shared spatial-fold assignment are used by all six evaluations (two model families $\times$ three variants), with model family, feature registry, preprocessing, hyper-parameters and seeds held fixed. Uncertainty is a paired spatial-block bootstrap on the model stage's own replicate draws with identical block draws across variants (1,000 replicates, seed 42, resampling unit \texttt{spatial\_block\_id}). The report states the analysis measures the closure date jointly with its interaction with the fixed MODIS seasonal production policy, not the closure date in isolation. Bejís, for scale: 12,814 cohort rows, 967 positives, 5 folds, 3,641 blocks. The shared folds are blocked at the pipeline's default 2-cell edge ($\approx$ 1 km): the analysis assigns block identifiers with \texttt{add\_spatial\_block\_id(cohort, spatial\_block\_size\_cells)} and takes that value from \texttt{STEP8B\_SPATIAL\_BLOCK\_SIZE\_CELLS = 2} (\texttt{repo/src/window\_closure\_sensitivity.py:8562}, \texttt{repo/core/config.py:556}). The comparison report records fold and block counts but not the block size, so this was read from the source rather than the report.

\subsubsection{Same-geography event-to-event comparison (Muğla 2021 versus 2022)}\label{sec:3.16.4}

Muğla is the one region for which a second fire event is analysed on the \textbf{identical} AOI and analysis grid (\texttt{region\_key = mugla\_aoi}, the same bounding box and the same $\sim$510 m cell definition), which allows the direction of feature-label associations to be compared with geography held fixed. The 2022 experiment is registered as \texttt{mugla\_2022\_event\_relative} with windows anchored to its own event: a 58-day predictor window (2022-04-24 $\rightarrow$ 2022-06-20) closing the day before ignition and a 49-day label window (2022-06-21 $\rightarrow$ 2022-08-08) opening on it, durations chosen to match the 2021 windows exactly (58 and 49 days).

\textbf{This is not a clean temporal-transfer design and is not presented as one.} The registry records the reason explicitly: the 2022 event ignites roughly five weeks earlier in the season than the 2021 event, so calendar year and seasonal phase are confounded and no difference can be attributed to the year alone. The registered claim is \texttt{same\_geography\_event\_to\_event}, and that is the claim made here. The entry is deliberately kept out of the canonical five-AOI cohort by its \texttt{temporal\_transfer\_wildfire} role so that a second year of an already-represented AOI cannot be silently enrolled into the spatial comparisons. That exclusion is not merely a convention we observe: it is enforced in code and tested. The ERA5-Land diagnostic's validator (\texttt{scripts/validate\_era5\_land\_regional\_diagnostic.py}) carries two relevant checks, and they have different reach. \texttt{A08\_cohort\_is\_the\_frozen\_five} requires the executed cohort to equal the frozen \texttt{DEFAULT\_EXPERIMENTS} tuple exactly, as an ordered comparison, so \emph{any} addition --- including this experiment --- fails it. \texttt{A07\_mugla\_2022\_absent\_from\_default\_analysis} is narrower than its name suggests: it tests literal membership of the string \texttt{mugla\_2022}, which is the registry's superseded calendar-shift record, and would not by itself catch the \texttt{mugla\_2022\_event\_relative} entry analysed here. Both checks pass on the executed output (Section~\ref{sec:3.17}), but the guarantee for this experiment rests on A08. The decision to keep this pair out of the 20-direction transfer matrix is therefore verifiable in the released code rather than resting on the text of this paper. The same leakage-safe pre-label exclusion applies as in every other region: cells that burned inside this experiment's own predictor window are removed from the analysis universe rather than counted as unburned.

Two frozen diagnostics are read for this pair, both produced by the machinery already described and neither refitting any model. Burned-pattern structure (component counts, effective component count, component-size and elevation distributions, land-cover mix) follows Section~\ref{sec:3.14.5}, computed on the primary population; outputs in \texttt{paper/mugla\_temporal\_raw/} with hashes in that directory's \texttt{SHA256SUMS.txt}. Signed univariate direction reversal follows Section~\ref{sec:3.12}: for each of the nine numeric features, the raw ROC-AUC of the feature against \texttt{burned} in each experiment, never folded to max(AUC, 1 $-$ AUC), so that a value below 0.5 is read as a direction rather than as weakness. Land cover is excluded from the AUC analysis because its integer class codes carry no meaningful scalar order, and is reported descriptively instead. Uncertainty is a spatial-block bootstrap on 10-cell ($\approx$ 5 km) blocks assigned before filtering, 1,000 replicates, seed 42, 2.5/97.5 percentile intervals; a reversal counts as bootstrap-supported only when both experiments' intervals exclude 0.5 on opposite sides. Outputs in \texttt{paper/step9g\_raw/} with hashes alongside. Four pair directories in that export carry a \texttt{\_superseded\_pre\_manavgat\_repair} suffix and are superseded; they are retained for the record and are not read here.

Unlike every other transfer direction in this paper, the two arms of this pair were not present in the frozen export delivered to us --- it contained no \texttt{mugla\_2021\_\_mugla\_2022\_event\_relative} directory --- so they were computed for this analysis. They were produced by running the project's own unmodified \texttt{src/step9b\_run\_cross\_region\_transfer.py} and \texttt{src/step9c\_cross\_region\_block\_bootstrap.py} at commit \texttt{48b56e7} --- the same code and the same protocol as Section~\ref{sec:3.10} and Section~\ref{sec:3.9}, with \texttt{random\_state = 42}, the primary RF configuration, and the 1,000-replicate spatial-block bootstrap on \texttt{spatial\_block\_id}. The frozen Step 8A modelling datasets of both experiments were the only inputs, hashed as read (\texttt{paper/mugla\_transfer\_raw/SHA256SUMS.txt}). Because \texttt{repo/} is treated as read-only and the pipeline resolves its paths from its own location, the run used a shadow project root containing a copy of \texttt{core/}, \texttt{src/} and \texttt{scripts/} plus those two inputs, so nothing was written into the pipeline repository or into the frozen output archive. The environment was Python 3.12.3 with scikit-learn 1.9.0, pandas 3.0.5 and NumPy 2.5.2, matching the version to which every other transfer number in this paper is fixed (Section~\ref{sec:4.7}e). One consequence is stated rather than hidden: the metrics file records \texttt{git\_commit: null}, because the shadow root is not itself a git repository.

\textbf{Independent execution of this pair.} These two directions were subsequently found to have been run by the pipeline author as well, in a separate environment and before our own run, and that export was supplied to us; the pair therefore rests on two independent executions rather than on one performed by the authors of this manuscript. The two runs are separated in date, machine, code-tree state and library stack: the pipeline author's run was produced on 2026-08-09 at commit \texttt{a07ea33} under scikit-learn 1.9.0 with pandas 3.0.2 and NumPy 2.4.4, and ours on 2026-08-11 at commit \texttt{48b56e7} under Python 3.12.3, scikit-learn 1.9.0, pandas 3.0.5 and NumPy 2.5.2. Both read the same two frozen Step 8A parquets, identical by SHA-256 (\texttt{c4ab107d…} for 2021 and \texttt{7c545f4d…} for the 2022 event-relative experiment), and both used \texttt{random\_state = 42}.

Agreement is to floating-point noise rather than to a stated tolerance. Across both directions and both model families the transfer ROC-AUC and PR-AUC point estimates agree to \textbf{$\le$1$\times$10$^{-7}$} --- the 2021$\rightarrow$2022 direction is bit-identical in every reported metric, and the largest discrepancy anywhere in the pair is 9.9$\times$10$^{-8}$ --- and the 1,000-replicate spatial-block bootstrap reproduces to the same order, with the $\Delta$AUC interval bounds agreeing to $\le$3.4$\times$10$^{-8}$. The agreement also holds below the metric level: the two runs' per-cell prediction tables have identical row counts and columns, and across all 295,402 predicted probabilities the largest absolute difference is 4.4$\times$10$^{-16}$, which is double-precision round-off. The prediction files themselves therefore differ in SHA-256 --- last-place decimal digits change the serialised string length --- while the human-readable step9b and step9c summary files of the two runs are byte-identical. The pipeline author's copy of these outputs is archived alongside ours in \texttt{paper/mugla\_transfer\_raw/emrehan\_run\_20260809/} with hashes and provenance in that directory's \texttt{SHA256SUMS.txt}. The interval-supported effects reported in Section~\ref{sec:4.8} are in any case an order of magnitude larger than the $\pm$0.02 to 0.03 cross-version tolerance of Section~\ref{sec:4.7}e, so the conclusions do not rest on the exact point estimates.

\subsection{Regional meteorological context (explanatory)}\label{sec:3.17}

To characterise the meteorological conditions each region actually experienced --- and specifically to test the post hoc explanation that Manavgat's outlying transfer behaviour reflects meteorological extremity (Section~\ref{sec:5.7}) --- an AOI-level ERA5-Land diagnostic was run outside the modelling pipeline (\texttt{src/era5\_land\_regional\_diagnostic.py}, with runner and validator in \texttt{scripts/}; outputs in \texttt{drive\_new/diagnostics/era5\_land\_regional/<analysis\_id>/}). It is explanatory only: it produces a table and exports no raster, and its outputs enter no feature set, no model and no transfer arm. The module records this status in its own output (\texttt{is\_model\_predictor: false}). The candidate diagnostic set of Section~\ref{sec:3.14} was fixed before any diagnostic-versus-transfer correlation was computed, and no meteorological measure is added to it; the reasoning is given in Section~\ref{sec:5.7}.

Hourly \texttt{temperature\_2m}, \texttt{dewpoint\_temperature\_2m}, \texttt{u\_component\_of\_wind\_10m}, \texttt{v\_component\_of\_wind\_10m} and \texttt{total\_precipitation\_hourly} are read from the ERA5-Land hourly reanalysis \citep{MunozSabater2021} as the Earth Engine collection \texttt{ECMWF/ERA5\_LAND/HOURLY}. Four variables are derived per pixel and per hour, never from window means: temperature (K $\rightarrow$ \textdegree{}C); relative humidity as 100·e\_s(T\_d)/e\_s(T) using the ECMWF/Tetens saturation formula over water for both terms (T$_{0}$ = 273.16 K, a$_{1}$ = 611.21 Pa, a$_{3}$ = 17.502, a$_{4}$ = 32.19 K), left unclipped and only checked for finiteness; wind speed as √(u10$^{2}$ + v10$^{2}$); and precipitation depth from the hourly accumulation band (m $\rightarrow$ mm), the cumulative \texttt{total\_precipitation} band never being used, so no differencing of a running total is involved.

Each hourly field is reduced to one AOI value by an explicit pixel-area weighting, Σ(value $\times$ pixelArea) / Σ(pixelArea), with the denominator masked by that variable's own mask so that a variable undefined over part of the AOI is not credited with that area. Both sums are evaluated on ERA5-Land's native projection and transform with \texttt{bestEffort=False}; an unweighted mean is not used. Window statistics are then computed over the resulting series of hourly regional means --- window mean and maximum for temperature, humidity and wind, and additionally the window total for precipitation --- so that a reported maximum is the most extreme regional hour, never the most extreme individual pixel.

The observed windows are each region's own predictor and label windows taken from the experiment registry (Section~\ref{sec:3.1}); no date is hard-coded in the diagnostic, and the registry's inclusive end date is converted exactly once to Earth Engine's exclusive bound. Each statistic is referenced to a climatology built by mapping the same calendar month-day window into the four reference years 2017 to 2020, computing each year's statistic independently, and taking their arithmetic mean and sample standard deviation (ddof = 1); the standardised anomaly is (observed $-$ climatological mean) / climatological SD, written as null --- never as zero or infinity --- when the climatological SD is exactly zero. Every window, observed and climatological alike, must contain the exact contiguous hourly UTC sequence (n\_days\_inclusive $\times$ 24 hours); a missing, duplicated, out-of-order, shifted or extra hour fails the run rather than being sorted, interpolated, padded or dropped. The cohort is the five canonical regions in a fixed order, Muğla 2022 being deliberately excluded, and the scientific configuration is hashed into the output namespace identifier so that a changed cohort or contract resolves to a different namespace rather than silently overwriting an existing result.

\textbf{Standardised anomalies are computed by the diagnostic but are not reported in this paper.} Two properties of the climatology make them unsuitable for the comparative use a reader would put them to. First, it spans only four years, so each standard deviation carries three degrees of freedom and is correspondingly unstable. Second, and decisively, the resulting standard deviations are strongly heterogeneous \emph{between} regions: over the five predictor windows the climatological SD spans 0.41 to 1.13 \textdegree{}C for temperature, 1.09 to 6.58 \% for relative humidity, 0.039 to 0.146 m s$^{-1}$ for wind speed and 12.6 to 48.0 mm for precipitation total --- ratios of 2.7$\times$ to 6.0$\times$, rising to 7.8$\times$ and 11.5$\times$ for temperature and precipitation in the label windows. A standardised anomaly therefore denotes a different physical departure in each region, and the cross-region comparison it invites is not meaningful. Anomalies are reported in physical units throughout (Section~\ref{sec:4.9}). The instability is not hypothetical: Bejís's label-window temperature and Muğla's predictor-window wind speed exceed five standardised units on climatological SDs of 0.147 \textdegree{}C and 0.065 m s$^{-1}$, from physical anomalies of only +0.83 \textdegree{}C and +0.34 m s$^{-1}$.

Correctness of the output was verified rather than assumed. The four files were obtained from the pipeline author, and their SHA-256 hashes match those recorded in the accompanying manifest (\texttt{paper/era5\_raw/SHA256SUMS.txt}); the analysis identifier agrees across the manifest, the contract and the containing namespace. The companion validator (\texttt{scripts/validate\_era5\_land\_regional\_diagnostic.py}) was then \textbf{executed against this output in \texttt{--mode actual}, and all 27 contract checks passed with none failed and none skipped}. Among them: the climatological mean and sample SD reproduce from the four retained yearly realisations (A20); observed windows and every climatological realisation are hourly complete (A25, A26); the standardised anomaly is null exactly when the climatological SD is zero (A16); the CSV and JSON summaries agree value by value (A17); the summary contains no infinite or missing quantity and no \texttt{Infinity}/\texttt{NaN} literal (A18, A19); the manifest hashes and byte sizes match (A21); the cohort is the frozen five with Muğla 2022 absent (A07, A08); the reference years and \texttt{sd\_ddof = 1} are as declared (A09, A10); the registry region keys and window dates agree with \texttt{core/regions.py} (A14); and the namespace contains only the four expected files, no exported raster having leaked into it (A24). The run was performed by the authors on 2026-08-11 under Python 3.12.3 with \texttt{earthengine-api} 1.7.39 installed solely to satisfy the module import chain --- the validator opens no Earth Engine session and requires no credentials --- with the repository at commit \texttt{48b56e7} and the outputs staged in a scratch namespace outside the repository via \texttt{--output-root}.

The manifest names commit \texttt{a07ea33}, at which neither the diagnostic source nor the Montiferru registry entry yet exists; both were first committed in \texttt{48b56e7}. The production run was therefore made from a working tree carrying uncommitted changes, and the recorded commit identifies only the last commit at run time. The code that actually ran can nevertheless be identified. The output contains Montiferru with its registry windows, which \texttt{a07ea33} cannot supply --- \texttt{core/regions.py} gains that entry only in \texttt{48b56e7}, and it does so by pure addition (529 lines inserted, none deleted), leaving the four regions common to both commits byte-identical. \texttt{core/paths.py} and \texttt{core/config.py}, the diagnostic's only other internal dependencies, are unchanged between the two commits. Every free-text semantics string hashed into the scientific contract matches \texttt{48b56e7} verbatim, and the validator's registry check (A14) confirms that all five regions' keys and window dates in the output agree with \texttt{48b56e7}'s registry. The working tree that produced this output therefore carried the registry and diagnostic content of \texttt{48b56e7}, which is the version described here and the version pinned as a submodule of the manuscript repository.

All five regions pass the admissibility gate as wildfire candidates (burned natural-vegetation fraction 0.723 to 0.991). Montiferru is the weakest pass, with a burned cropland fraction of 0.274; its sensitivity to this composition is examined in Section~\ref{sec:4.7}b. The negative control behaves as designed: in Kozan 2023 the gate classifies 542 burned cells as 0.017 natural vegetation and 0.983 cropland (533 of 542 burned cells cropland-dominant, 8 grassland, 1 tree cover), returning the verdict \emph{cropland-dominated control}, and the region is excluded from all modelling. The separation is not marginal --- the five admitted regions carry natural-vegetation fractions of 0.723 to 0.991 against the control's 0.017, so the 0.50 threshold falls in an empty interval rather than between neighbouring cases. This establishes that the gate discriminates burned area produced by natural-fuel combustion from burned area produced by post-harvest stubble burning, which MCD64A1 itself does not distinguish, and that admission of the five study regions is a decision the data supports rather than a selection made by hand.

North Evia is analysed on an extended AOI. Relative to the legacy 0.40\textdegree{}$\times$0.40\textdegree{} box, the extended 0.80\textdegree{}$\times$0.60\textdegree{} box ($\sim$3$\times$ the area, identical predictor and label windows) leaves the burned scar essentially unchanged (2,789 $\rightarrow$ 2,803 burned cells) while cutting overall prevalence from 0.361 to 0.122 and TSG prevalence from 0.676 to 0.287. The effect of this choice on transfer is reported in Section~\ref{sec:4.7}a.

In every region, adding the six thermal predictors to the static baseline increases spatially blocked out-of-fold ROC-AUC, and the increment's bootstrap interval excludes zero at every block size tested (Table~\ref{tab:3}; [Fig.~\ref{fig:within-robustness}]).

Absolute AUC declines as blocks coarsen, as expected when long-range spatial structure is progressively withheld, but the increment itself does not erode toward zero: at 20-cell ($\sim$10 km) blocking $\Delta$AUC remains between +0.048 and +0.154 with all intervals above zero. The same holds in the secondary all-valid population (Section~\ref{sec:4.7}f).

\textbf{Raw transfer is heterogeneous and includes anti-predictive directions.} Raw target AUC spans 0.326 to 0.686. Twelve of 20 directions are above chance with CI support, six are \emph{below} chance with CI support (both directions of Manavgat$\leftrightarrow$Bejís and Manavgat$\leftrightarrow$Muğla, plus Bejís$\rightarrow$Evia and Evia$\rightarrow$Bejís), and two intervals span 0.5. Even the best raw transfer (Evia$\rightarrow$Manavgat, 0.686) remains far below the target's own within-region thermal performance (0.870); across all directions the raw deficit against the within-region reference is 0.184 to 0.592 AUC.

\textbf{The thermal block's transfer contribution is sign-unstable per direction.} Pairing each direction's thermal model against the static baseline model under the same protocol (Table~\ref{tab:R6}) shows that the block worth +0.056 to +0.153 AUC inside every region is worth +0.004 on average across regions: its paired contribution is CI-supported positive in 10 directions, CI-supported negative in 7, and uncertain in 3. It is the swing factor at the chance line --- adding the thermal block drags three directions from a baseline at or above chance to below it (Manavgat$\rightarrow$Muğla 0.508 $\rightarrow$ 0.470; Bejís$\rightarrow$Evia 0.531 $\rightarrow$ 0.383; Muğla$\rightarrow$Manavgat 0.522 $\rightarrow$ 0.401) and lifts one from below to above (Muğla$\rightarrow$Bejís 0.451 $\rightarrow$ 0.583). In the Manavgat-Muğla pair the baseline transfers at roughly chance and the thermal block pushes both directions below it; in the Bejís-Muğla pair the thermal block is what carries transfer above chance in both directions.

The decomposition ([Fig.~\ref{fig:adaptation}]) shows both faces of the same behaviour. In the five directions where raw transfer was below chance, the best label-blind method recovers at most 34\% of the gap to the within-region reference; the remaining (concept) fraction is at least 0.66 everywhere. Seven directions show \emph{negative} recovery --- adaptation moves the score away from the within-region reference, in the worst case (Evia$\rightarrow$Manavgat) recovering $-$0.86 of the gap. In six of the seven, raw transfer was already above chance and adaptation destroyed that advantage; in the seventh (Manavgat$\rightarrow$Muğla), raw transfer was below chance (0.470) and adaptation lowered it further (0.443). Label-blind adaptation therefore does not act as a repair mechanism: it compresses all directions toward chance, closing a minority of the deficit where transfer fails and destroying performance where transfer works.

\emph{Table note (power): the effective sample is 10 unordered pairs (6 for the 12-direction rows; 8 for the supported-conditional rows); the two directions of a pair are not independent and every pair shares regions with three others. Intervals of width $\pm$0.5 to 0.8 cannot rule out moderate true correlations; null rows are "not shown to order transfer", not "shown not to".}

Of the 20 variants, exactly two have bootstrap intervals excluding zero, and both belong to the conditional family: the sign-agreement fraction over CI-supported features ($\rho$ = +0.84 [+0.58, +0.88]) and the cosine similarity of supported signed-AUC vectors ($\rho$ = +0.81 [+0.33, +0.88]) (Section~\ref{sec:3.14.4}). These indices are computed from signed feature-response directions in \emph{both} regions and therefore require burned labels (or a labelled probe) in the target; unlike every P(x), P(x|y=1) and P(y) row, they are not label-free.

The remaining families all fail to order the matrix. The domain classifier (Section~\ref{sec:3.14.2}) is at ceiling for every pair (AUC 0.962 to 0.9999) --- marginal shift is essentially total everywhere --- so it cannot discriminate outcomes ranging from 0.33 to 0.69. The canonical SDM niche-overlap instruments (Schoener's D, Warren's I, Mahalanobis distance between burned-cell distributions; Section~\ref{sec:3.14.3}) span $\rho$ $-$0.23 to +0.24 with all intervals crossing zero. Fire-regime structure (Section~\ref{sec:3.14.5}) has the \emph{wrong-signed} point estimate ($\rho$ +0.29): the most regime-similar pair (Bejís-Evia, effective component count 1.0000 vs 1.0083) fails in both directions while the most regime-different pair (Bejís-Muğla) transfers above chance. At pair level, niche overlap and sign agreement are empirically distinct ($\rho$ between them $-$0.36 to +0.45, all CIs spanning zero), and in partial rank correlations the conditional index retains its association with transfer with niche overlap held fixed (partial $\rho$ +0.82 [+0.40, +0.88]) while niche overlap retains none with the conditional index held fixed ($-$0.07 [$-$0.39, +0.37]).

The clearest single view of the preceding table is a two-pair contrast ([Fig.~\ref{fig:contrast-pairs}]; per-feature data in \texttt{figure\_contrast\_pairs.csv}). [Production note: the OUTLINE slot reserved for signed univariate AUC per feature with CIs is realised by Fig.~\ref{fig:contrast-pairs} --- two panels of per-feature signed AUC with $\sim$5 km-block CIs, one per pair, annotated with the overlap and transfer numbers below.]

  \label{tab:R2}
  \begin{tabular}{lll}
    \hline
     & Manavgat ~ Muğla & Bejís ~ Montiferru \\
    \hline
    Schoener's D̄ (1-D, 9 features) & \textbf{0.826} --- highest of all 10 pairs & \textbf{0.479} --- lowest of all 10 pairs \\
    Mahalanobis (burned centroids) & 2.71 (closest) & 8.11 (farthest) \\
